subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that sin 20° sin 40° sin 60° sin 80° = 3/16.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 39(iii), book p.92. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The two marks sit on applying the product identity and on the closing multiplication; spotting the 60° ± 20° pattern stays on the page as unmarked working. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1-Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, and Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. NUMERIC CHECK before authoring: the product was evaluated to 12 decimal places as 0.187500000000, which is exactly 3/16. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this one — name the formula you use and how you finish.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Spot the 60° pattern
steps.margin_note: Take sin 60° out first. What is left is sin A, sin(60° − A) and sin(60° + A) with A = 20°.

recall.must_convey: That 40° = 60° − 20° and 80° = 60° + 20°, so three factors form sin A sin(60° − A) sin(60° + A) with A = 20°.
accept: forty and eighty are twenty either side of sixty
keep sin sixty aside and bracket the other three
the bracket is sin a sin sixty minus a sin sixty plus a with a as twenty
sixty ki rendu vaipula twenty untundi

steps.why: Three of the four angles are 20° and 60° either side of it, which is exactly the shape of the standard product identity. sin 60° is set aside as a separate factor.
common_mistakes: Trying to work out sin 20°, sin 40° and sin 80° as decimals.
Including sin 60° inside the bracket as well.
steps.memory_tip: 40° and 80° sit 20° either side of 60°, so the bracket is the standard triple product.

steps.label: Apply the product identity
steps.margin_note: First mark. Quote the identity, then put A = 20° so that 3A = 60°. Three unknown sines become one known sine.
lines: sin A sin(60° − A) sin(60° + A)

recall.must_convey: That sin A sin(60° − A) sin(60° + A) = (1/4) sin 3A, so with A = 20° the bracket is (1/4) sin 60°.
accept: sin a sin sixty minus a sin sixty plus a is one by four sin three a
with a as twenty the angle three a is sixty
the bracket becomes a quarter of sin sixty
a equal twenty pettithe three a sixty avthundi
use the triple angle product identity
reject: the answer is three by sixteen

steps.why: The identity replaces three sines of awkward angles by a single sine of 3A. With A = 20° that single angle is 60°, whose value is known.
common_mistakes: Using (1/4) sin A instead of (1/4) sin 3A.
steps.memory_tip: The three angles A, 60° − A, 60° + A give a quarter of sin 3A.

steps.label: Multiply by sin 60°
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Bring back the sin 60° set aside at the start. Two copies of √3/2 give 3/4, and a quarter of 3/4 is 3/16.

accept: sin sixty is root three by two and it appears twice
root three by two squared is three by four
a quarter of three by four is three by sixteen
root three by two rendu sarlu vasthundi
the answer is three by sixteen
reject: use the triple angle product identity

steps.why: The factor sin 60° that was set aside now meets the sin 60° produced by the identity, so √3/2 appears twice and squares to 3/4.
common_mistakes: Using sin 60° only once and getting √3/8.
steps.memory_tip: √3/2 appears twice, and squaring it gives 3/4. A quarter of 3/4 is 3/16.
